El Niño and its impact on the global energy system

Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have climbed to a record high for the time of year, causing forecasters to predict a very strong El Niño will form in the final months of 2026.  

Surface temperatures averaged about 29.6°C last week, up from 26.6°C at the same time last year, according to data from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. 

Temperatures were 1°C higher than the previous record for the time of year and 2.7°C above the long-term seasonal average, indicating exceptional warmth across the region. 

Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific are a key driver of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon, the single largest influence on weather patterns at seasonal scale worldwide. 

ENSO has significant impacts on the energy production and consumption – including hurricane formation in the Atlantic, winter temperatures and heating demand in the United States, and hydroelectric generation in South America ...

#Commodities
#Gold surged more than 4% to challenge the 200-day moving average at USD 4,511, its largest single-day gain in six months and its highest level since early June. The move was driven by the sharp fall in the dollar and long-end Treasury yields following the buyback announcement, with analysts noting the rally also reflects a growing market premium on US institutional and policy volatility.

Brent #crudeoil held above $91 per barrel into Thursday’s session, extending a four-day run of gains as President Trump announced sweeping new economic measures against Iran and the UAE cut trade and financial ties with Tehran. Meanwhile, there are signs that some crude from other Persian Gulf producers is being covertly ferried out through Hormuz despite threats to shipping. In the US, refineries are processing the most crude since 2019 while nationwide distillate stocks continue to tumble, hitting a 1996 seasonal low in EIA’s latest report.

#Copper received a boost from the weaker dollar while the historic LME squeeze continued to ease, with the cash-to-three-month backwardation falling to around $248 per metric ton from a peak of $545 earlier in the week, after Trafigura and other traders made significant metal deliveries to the exchange, thereby easing a squeeze on supplies after being drained by a surge in shipments to the US ahead of a potential tariff announcement. HG Copper traded near USD 6.50 after finding support around the 50-day moving average at USD 6.39.

Key takeaways from the latest EIA report:

US crude inventories rose 4.4 million barrels, despite crude exports jumping by around 1 mb/d to back above 4 mb/d. Another 5.3 million barrels was released from the SPR, lifting the cumulative draw during the Iran war to around 122 million barrels and continuing to cushion the domestic market from the global supply disruption.

Refinery runs surged to 17.4 mb/d, the highest since September 2019, led by increased Gulf Coast activity. Refiners continue to run hard amid tight refined-product supplies and exceptionally strong margins, particularly for middle distillates.

Distillate inventories fell another 1.5 million barrels to their lowest seasonal level since 1996. The continued draw is particularly notable with the Northern Hemisphere winter heating season approaching, leaving the market with a limited inventory buffer and helping explain the persistent strength in diesel cracks.

Gasoline provided the weak spot, with implied demand falling to 8.9 mb/d, its lowest seasonal level since pandemic-hit 2020.
